issues.item: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
issues.explanation: This item is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the cognitive formulation. The active formulation is dominated by a Triggers–Threat–Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Negative Appraisals inactive. In contrast, punishment/self-deserving-suffering is a negative self-appraisal theme rather than a threat-management strategy, and it does not connect plausibly to the selected trigger and threat items. The other maladaptive strategies (avoiding emotional stress, staying near exits) fit the trigger-threat-hypervigilance pattern, but punishment thinking pulls toward a different clinical profile that is otherwise not represented.

vignette:
Carlos, a sixty-five-year-old special education teacher, had spent most of his adult life trying not to think about the afternoon in the jungle that had left him with a taste he could still summon on his tongue. He was twenty-two then, a squad leader in a hot, humid place that maps called one thing and his memory called something else. An ambush, a burst of automatic fire, and then-nothing, until he woke flat on his back, staring into the canopy, a medic leaning over him. The taste of blood and copper filled his mouth, mixed with the grit of soil and the metallic residue of his own fear. His ears rang, and the world swayed under him when he tried to sit up. He had never told anyone that the dizziness returned sometimes, or that certain foods-especially rare beef or a particular brand of mint-made the taste flood back, as fresh as if the medic were still pressing gauze into his cheek. But he had been forced to talk about it once, during a routine physical at the VA clinic three years ago. The physician asked, as the form required, "Any combat exposure?" and Carlos had answered in short, flat sentences: ambush, wounded, evacuated. As he spoke, the copper taste bloomed in his mouth, the room began to tilt, and he had to grip the edge of the exam table to keep from sliding off. The doctor noticed his pallor and asked if he felt okay. Carlos said he was fine, but for the rest of the day he could not shake the sensation that the jungle was just outside the clinic window, waiting.

After the divorce, which his ex-wife had attributed to his "inability to be present," Carlos moved into a small apartment near the elementary school where he had worked for thirty years. The classroom became his refuge, but also his daily trial. He taught a group of six children with emotional and behavioral disorders, a job that required patience and a calm demeanor. Yet he had learned that strong emotions-a child's screaming tantrum, a frustrated colleague's raised voice-triggered a sensation he could only describe as the walls closing in. He avoided situations that felt charged, even if it meant missing team meetings or asking a paraprofessional to handle a student in crisis. His colleagues noticed, but they called him "private" and left him alone. Once, during a staff development day, a presenter asked the group to share a personal story about resilience. Carlos felt his chest tighten, the copper taste rising, and he silently shook his head when the facilitator's eyes met his. He had come to believe that even naming what happened brought the event too close-that the memory was a trap door, and talking about it was the step that opened it.

Every morning, Carlos entered his classroom and automatically scanned the room: the door, the windows, the placement of furniture. He always sat with his back to the wall, facing the entrance, and made sure his route to the door was clear. During fire drills, he found himself already calculating the fastest exit before the alarm sounded. The alarm itself-that sudden loud siren-sent his heart slamming against his ribs, and he would have to grip the edge of his desk to keep from bolting out of the building. He had come to believe that disaster was always possible, that the safe moment was an illusion, and that his only protection was constant watchfulness. The sound was not the worst part, though. What he dreaded more was the inevitable conversation afterward-a well-meaning coworker asking, "You okay? You looked scared." That question forced him to talk about it, even indirectly, and he had learned that any sustained attention to his state could summon the taste, the sway, the sense of being back in the hot, wet air.

The consequences of this vigilance had accumulated over the years. He had stopped going to restaurants because he could not enjoy a meal while plotting the nearest exit or scanning the room for signs of trouble. He declined invitations to social gatherings, especially those involving loud music or unpredictable crowds. His relationship with his adult daughter had grown distant because he could not tolerate her emotional intensity, her tears or her laughter, which he found disorienting and vaguely dangerous. At work, his principal had recently expressed concern about his "hypervigilance" and suggested he see a counselor after a reported incident: during a classroom assembly, a child accidentally knocked over a sound system, and Carlos had dropped to the floor, eyes wide, before excusing himself to the restroom. He could not bring himself to explain that the loud crack had tasted like copper and metal, had spun the room around him, had brought back a jungle he had never really left. The principal, a kind woman, had asked him directly, "Was it something from your time in the service?" and Carlos had nodded, unable to speak. He felt the dizziness start, the familiar metallic film coating his tongue, and he had to sit down.

It was the principal's concern, combined with a growing sense that he was losing control of his own classroom, that finally drove Carlos to schedule an appointment at a community mental health clinic. He sat in the waiting room with his back to the wall, counting the exits, and when the therapist called his name, he felt the familiar stir of dizziness. He knew that at some point he would have to talk about the event in detail-that was what therapy was, after all-and the prospect made him nauseous. What he hoped for was simple: a way to sit through a staff meeting without feeling like he was under fire. What he feared was the same thing he had feared for over forty years-that the taste would return, the world would tilt, and there would be no medic this time, only the slow unraveling of the quiet life he had built so carefully around the silence. And yet, a part of him wondered if maybe talking about it, really talking about it, could finally drain the copper from his mouth and let him breathe.
